title: How a Husband-Wife Duo Built Victoria's First South Indian Restaurant Into a Two-Location Success
excerpt: Dosa Paragon, which started as a tiny storefront on Yates Street in Victoria, BC, has expanded to a second location and earned a loyal following for its crispy dosas and authentic South Indian cooking.
body:
• Dosa Paragon, run by a husband-and-wife team, was Victoria's first dedicated South Indian restaurant and now operates two locations in the city's downtown.
  • The restaurant has earned ratings above 4.5 stars across major review platforms, with customers praising its authentic dosas, sambar, and South Indian thalis.
  • Dosa Paragon recently offered a special Onam Sadya feast — a traditional Kerala banana-leaf meal — priced at $32.99 for takeout, connecting Vancouver Island's Indian community to seasonal traditions.
  • The restaurant was recently featured on CHEK News' Order Up segment, highlighting its growing profile in British Columbia's food scene.

On a quiet stretch of Yates Street in downtown Victoria, British Columbia, a husband-and-wife team set out to fill a gap no one else had addressed: the city had no dedicated South Indian restaurant. Dosa Paragon changed that, and has since grown from a single storefront into a two-location operation with a devoted following.

The restaurant now serves from both its original spot at 735 Yates Street and a second location at 1218 Wharf Street, offering a menu built around the staples of South Indian cooking — crispy dosas stuffed with potato masala, fluffy idlis with sambar and coconut chutney, crunchy vadas, and a rotating selection of curries that span the subcontinent's southern states.

Authenticity as the Business Model

In a Canadian dining market where Indian food often defaults to butter chicken and naan, Dosa Paragon has staked its identity on regional specificity. The menu reads like a tour of South Indian kitchens: Mysore masala dosa, kothu parotta, Madras chicken curry, and Chettinad lamb sit alongside Indo-Chinese fusion dishes and Kerala parathas.

The approach has earned consistently high marks. The restaurant holds a 4.4-star rating across more than 1,000 reviews on Uber Eats at its Wharf Street location, and a 4.9-star rating on independent review platforms at the Yates Street original. Reviewers frequently cite the crispness of the dosas, the depth of the sambar, and the reasonable prices — most dishes fall between $6 and $24 — as reasons they keep coming back.

"If you're craving authentic South Indian food in Victoria, Dosa Paragon is the place to go. It's hands down the best spot in town for dosa — crispy, flavorful, and always satisfying," one reviewer wrote on Wanderlog. Another compared the experience to eating in India itself: "The taste, flavor, and crispness are exactly like the dosas I used to enjoy back in India."

Celebrating Onam on Vancouver Island

The restaurant recently underscored its cultural roots with a special Onam Sadya menu, offered for $32.99 as a takeout-only feast on August 23 from the Wharf Street location. The traditional Kerala harvest celebration meal — served on a banana leaf and featuring rice, curries, thoran, pachadi, pickles, chips, pappadam, and payasam — is the kind of offering that turns a restaurant into a community anchor.

For the Indian diaspora on Vancouver Island, where South Asian populations are smaller than in Vancouver or Toronto, having access to a properly executed sadya marks Dosa Paragon as more than a casual eatery. It is a cultural touchpoint, connecting families to seasonal traditions thousands of miles from home.

From Local Gem to Regional Spotlight

The restaurant was recently featured on CHEK News' Order Up segment, a local television series that highlights standout dining options across Vancouver Island. The coverage reflects a growing profile that has taken Dosa Paragon beyond word-of-mouth and into the broader British Columbia food conversation.

In a city better known for fish and chips and farm-to-table dining, a husband-and-wife duo serving crispy dosas and banana-leaf feasts have carved out something rare: a restaurant that feels like home for one community while introducing another to flavors they never knew they were missing.
